client: I’ve been feeling so much pressure ever since I got that disappointing grade on my final project last semester. I’m terrified of losing my scholarship this term, and it’s hard to focus because I keep thinking about how much is at stake. Honestly, I’m not sure if talking about it here will really help—it feels like the problem is just there, no matter what.
therapist: It sounds like that disappointing grade has really shaken your confidence and created a lot of anxiety about the future. I hear how overwhelming it feels when your mind keeps circling back to those worries—that must be exhausting. What do you notice happens to your ability to focus when those anxious thoughts come up?

client: When those anxious thoughts come up, I just freeze. I sit down to study, but I can’t concentrate because I’m so worried about failing again. It feels like no matter how much I try, I’m just going to mess things up. I don’t know how to stop feeling this way—it’s like my brain won’t let me move forward.
therapist: That "freezing" sensation and the belief that you'll mess up again must feel incredibly paralyzing. It's understandable that studying becomes so difficult when you're caught in that cycle of worry. What do you think might happen if you tried breaking your study time into much smaller, more manageable chunks?

client: I guess smaller chunks might help, but I’ve tried that before and still ended up panicking. It feels like no matter how I split my time, the anxiety creeps in anyway. What if I still fail even with small study sessions? That thought makes my chest tighten.
therapist: I hear how even breaking work down hasn't fully eased that fear of failure yet—that must feel so discouraging when you're trying so hard. That physical tightness in your chest shows how real these worries feel for you. What do you notice tends to make the anxiety feel slightly more manageable, even if just a little?

client: Sometimes if I call my sister before studying, it helps for maybe 10 minutes. But then I start thinking she's just trying to make me feel better and doesn't really understand how serious this is. I don't know why temporary distractions work sometimes but never last. It's frustrating.
therapist: It sounds like connecting with your sister provides a brief sense of comfort, even if the relief doesn’t last long—that’s still a meaningful step. I hear your frustration when those moments of calm feel fleeting, and it’s understandable to question whether others truly grasp the weight of your situation. What do you think it would feel like to hold onto that small bit of relief, even if it’s temporary, without judging it as not enough?

client: Holding onto that small relief without judging it feels... hard. I think part of me feels like it’s not enough because I’m still facing the same big problem. I worry that if I focus on the small moments, I’ll just be avoiding the real issue. But I guess I don’t know how to balance acknowledging those moments while still dealing with the bigger fear of failing.
therapist: You're describing such an important tension—wanting to appreciate those small moments of relief while also needing to address the very real fears about your future. It makes sense that this balance feels tricky to find. What do you imagine might happen if you saw those brief calm moments not as avoidance, but as small steps in building your resilience to face the bigger challenges?

client: That way of looking at it is different... I guess I never thought of the calm moments as actually helping me face the bigger anxiety. But part of me worries it's too simplistic—like those moments don't actually change the fact that my scholarship is still at risk. It's hard to trust that small things could add up when the stakes feel so high.
therapist: You're absolutely right that those small moments don't change the objective reality of your scholarship situation—that's very perceptive of you to notice. What if we thought of them less as a solution and more like briefly catching your breath while climbing a steep hill? How does that metaphor land for you?

client: That metaphor makes sense, but catching my breath doesn't feel like enough when I'm still staring up at this huge hill. It's hard to believe those brief moments of calm could make a difference when the climb ahead still feels so impossible. I don't mean to be negative, I just don't know how to trust that small things matter when the big picture still feels overwhelming.
therapist: It sounds like while the metaphor resonates, there's still a big gap between understanding these small moments intellectually and truly feeling their value when facing such significant challenges. That struggle to trust in small steps when the mountain looms large is completely understandable. What would need to shift, even just a tiny bit, for those breathing moments to feel slightly more meaningful alongside the climb?

client: Maybe if I could see one small study session where I actually retained information and didn't panic the whole time... that might help a little. But even as I say that, I worry that one good session won't mean anything if I can't keep it up. I'm so used to expecting the worst that it's hard to let small successes count for anything.
therapist: It sounds like you're starting to identify what might help—a small study session where you feel focused and in control—while also recognizing how quickly that hopeful thought gets overshadowed by doubts about sustaining it. That pattern of anticipating the worst, even when considering small successes, must feel really discouraging. What would it be like to try just one focused session and notice what happens without immediately judging whether you can keep it up?

client: I could try one focused session, but I’m afraid I’ll just end up feeling worse if it doesn’t go well. It’s hard to approach it without judging myself because I’m so used to expecting failure. I don’t know how to separate noticing what happens from immediately jumping to conclusions about what it means for the future.
therapist: That fear of feeling worse if it doesn't go perfectly shows how much pressure you're putting on these small attempts—it makes complete sense that you'd approach them cautiously. You've described such an important insight about how quickly noticing turns into judging when you're used to expecting failure. What would it feel like to approach this session as simply gathering information, rather than a test you can pass or fail?

client: That actually makes me feel a little less tense—thinking of it as gathering information instead of passing or failing. But old habits are hard to break. Part of me still worries that if I don't see immediate progress during that session, it'll just confirm my fears. It's exhausting to constantly battle between wanting to try this new approach and expecting the worst.
therapist: It sounds like you're experiencing that push-pull between hope and familiar doubt—both wanting this new perspective to help while bracing for disappointment. That mental exhaustion is completely understandable when you've been stuck in this cycle for so long. What do you notice happens in your body when you consider approaching this session as information-gathering rather than a pass/fail test?
